title: Oct. 22 - Daily Music
body:
Today's music recommendation is *Tezeta (Nostalgia)* by Mulatu Astatke from *Ethiopiques, Vol. 4: Ethio Jazz 1969-1974*. 

"Musically trained in London and schooled in the club scene of mid-'60s New York, Mulatu Astatke stands as the exceptional musical innovator of the Ethiopian groove. Starting in 1969, he created the first bands independent of the military, which had previously dominated the country's music scene. Having immersed himself in Caribbean music, funk, jazz and Latin grooves during his lengthy stint abroad, Mulatu returned to his native land to give rise to a brand new sound. An album of instrumentals, Ethiopiques Volume 4 is a case study in the inventive blending of influences that comprised the Ethiopian groove. Strains of funk and reggae timings permeate the thick and chunky bass lines, which are pushed prominently forward in the mix. Multiple saxophones swirl with the hypnotic, snake-charming sounds of the East, while at the same time resonating with jazzy tones reminiscent of John Coltrane and Lester Young. Guitar is a main ingredient here, growling with funky distorted wah-pedaled fuzz riffs that sound like they were lifted straight out of an early '70s black-exploitation flick. Drums and percussion combine the punchy funk of James Brown and the Meters with the heavy Latin rhythms of Mongo Santamaria and Willie Bobo. Fusing all of these elements together, Mulatu unleashes a potent brew of afro-jazz grooves that pull you in and leave you in a mystical trance-like state. Whew! Even when the record stops, these mood-inspiring sounds linger on like a drug. Get your head on right, light a candle, sit back, and you too will understand...Tropical in its roots, funky and intoxicating in its impact, Mulatu Astatke's distinct brand of Ethiopian music features some of the most soulful hip-grinding instrumentals ever recorded in Mother Africa." - John Ballon

title: A Summary of Three Years of Yoyoing
Oct. 25 - Daily Music
body:
Today's music recommendation is *Mladic* by Godspeed You! Black Emperor from *Allelujah! Don't Bend! Ascend!*. 

"The two lengthy tracks on Allelujah!, "Mladic" and "We Drift Like Worried Fire", have been part of the band's live repertoire since 2003. So the record feels in one sense like Godspeed taking care of unfinished business, presenting existing music from their influential run in a context that showcases its full force and power. Taken together, those tracks serve as a 40-minute summary of everything that made this band great. "Mladic" is all gloom and menace, building from an opening vocal snippet, adding pings of guitar, strings that saw away in a Middle Eastern mode, and dark clouds of feedback. This is the Godspeed that learned so much from the pummeling repetition of Swans and the fiendish drama of metal. There's not exactly hope in a track like "Mladic", but there is a kind of darkly shaded catharsis. Godspeed have never sounded quite this heavy, and it's especially impressive in how far it can veer from the themes that hold it together without losing the thread." - Pitchfork

"The opening track, “Mladic”, presumably named after the Bosnian war criminal Ratko Mladić, is a departure for them. Elements from the unreleased, yet long bootlegged track, “Albanian” have been fleshed out into the, by a wide margin, most aggressively rock track in the GY!BE catalog. It is, however, hardly standard or ordinary. And instead of their traditional, almost organized chaos, the strings of Sophie Trudeau unite with the guitars of Efrim Menuck and returning member Michael Moya to play one gigantic riff in the heart of the piece. The brilliant section has a reprise about ¾ of the way through. Closing with the sounds of a street parade, “Mladic” is an instantly gratifying masterpiece. Only one track in but it consumed twenty glorious minutes." - David Musto

title: Oct. 28 - Daily Music
body:
Today's music recommendation is *Piano Concerto "Memo Flora" (Op. 67)* by Takeshi Yoshimatsu. 

"Japanese composer, columnist and iconoclast Takashi Yoshimatsu evokes babbling brooks, chirping birds, and delicate beauty in this radically pastoral album featuring Sachio Fujioka and the Manchester Camerata. Yoshimatsu calls this aesthetic 'New Lyricism,' a style that seeks to refine contemporary classical music by stripping away the rougher edges of the avant-garde, making music that's beautiful for beauty's sake. But the crown jewel of the album, to my ears, is the namesake of the album, Yoshimatsu's Piano Concerto, 'Memo Flora.' 'Memo Flora' represents the absolute summit of Yoshimatsu's 'New Lyricism,' making use of the full range of color available in the orchestral palette. And this is a beautiful concerto; romantic enough to give Rachmaninoff a run for his money, expressive enough to confuse the sound of the orchestra for the outdoors at times, and novel enough to reward repeated listening with its rich spectrum of sonic variation. Yoshimatsu really pulls out all of the stops for the sake of one goal — beauty. This album is an excellent display of Yoshimatsu at his best and in his element; musing symphonically on nature." - William Peacock

"This is a perfect piano concerto for the month of August. Takashi Yoshimatsu is not the most well known composer, which is all the more reason to popularise his music. Memo Flora is about plants, and is in three parts: 1. Flower (Allegro) 2. Petals (Andante) 3. Bloom (Rondo in 4/8 and 5/8). Overall, Memo Flora is poised, intricate, but demonstrates a strength in resilience which is typical of the vegetative soul. It contains art, optimism and tragedy in every bar. It is quite possible however, that Yoshimatsu could do with a botany lesson because the progression flower > petals > bloom is not quite developmentally correct, or even indicates the full range of plant life. Imagine what a masterpiece we would have if he had decided to write a concerto on seeds > saplings > flower > fruition > death and rebirth. Of course, it is easy to criticise from the sidelines whilst the master creates, so instead I will leave you to the music to fold it into your own fertile imaginings and enjoyment." - The Bohemian Budgie

title: Why is the absolute value interesting?
body:
Many mathematics is built upon the notion of distance, whether from a geometric sense of the distance between lines or points, or from an algebraic sense of the distance between two numbers. The absolute value function, defined by 
$$
|x| = 
\begin{cases}
x & \text{if } x \geq 0 \\ 
-x & \text{if } x< 0
\end{cases}
$$
is how close a real number is to $0$ on the number line, so it is a kind of distance defined on the real numbers. In fact. we can write $|x-y|$ to be the distance between any two real numbers. 

To construct a distance on any set, we first develop the notion of a norm, which is defined as follows. 
\begin{definition}
A map $\|\cdot\|:K \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ on a field $K$ is a **norm** on $K$ if the following conditions are satisfied.
1. **Positive Definiteness**: $\|v\| \geq 0$ for all $v \in K$ and $\|v\| = 0$ iff $v = 0$.
2. **Multiplicativity**: $\|uv\| = \|u\|\cdot\|v\|$ for all $u,v \in K$.
3. **Triangle Inequality**: $\|u+v\| \leq \|u\| + \|v\|$ for all $u,v \in K$.
\end{definition}
A norm is a nonnegative real value assigned to any element of a field, and the usual absolute value is an example on $\mathbb{R}$.

Similarly, we abstract the definition of a distance or metric function.
\begin{definition}
A map of $d:M^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ over a set $V$ is a **metric** on $M$ if the following conditions are satisfied. 
1.  **Positivity**: $d(x,y) \geq 0$ for all $x,y \in M$ and $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$
2. **Symmetry**: $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$ for all $x,y \in M$
3. **Triangle Inequality**: $d(x,z) \leq d(x,y) + d(y,z)$ for all $x,y,z \in M$
\end{definition}
The absolute value is also an example of metrics. If we define the $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ between two real numbers $x,y$, then the function $d$ is a metric function. 

In fact, every norm can be generalized to a distance. Let $||\cdot||$ be a norm on $M$, then define the map $d(x,y) = ||x-y||$ for all $x,y \in M$. Then
1. The map $d$ follows positivity since $d(x,y) = ||x-y|| \geq 0$ following from positive definiteness of $||\cdot||$. Also, $||x-y|| = 0$ iff $x-y = 0$ or $x = y$. 
2. The map $d$ follows symmetry since \[d(x,y) = ||x-y|| = ||(-1)(y-x)|| = |-1|||y-x|| = 1\cdot ||y-x|| = ||y-x|| = d(y,x).\]
3. The map $d$ follows triangle inequality since  \[d(x,z) = ||x-z|| = ||(x-y)+(y-z)|| \leq ||x-y|| + ||y-z|| = d(x,y) + d(y,z).\]
so the norm $||\cdot||$ derives the metric $d$.

The mathematical definition of norm and metric can apply to all vector spaces, including functions for instance. The space of continuous functions on $[0,1]$ is a vector space for example, denoted by $C([0,1])$. Since this is a vector space, we can also construct norms on it. One example is the so-called $L^{\infty}$ norm, where for all $f \in C([0,1])$
\[||f||_{\infty} =  \sup_{x \in [0,1]} |f(x)|\]
There is also the $L^1$ norm where for all $f \in C([0,1])$
\[||f||_1 = \int_0^1 |f(x)| dx\]
Other interesting norms include the **[Hamming distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamming_distance)** (to 0) commonly used in information theory. 

There is one last norm I want to mention, which is the **p-adic norm** defined on $\mathbb{Q}$. The p-adic norm (p is a prime) of any $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ is defined to be $|q|_p = p^{-v_p(q)}$, where $v_p(q)$ is the p-adic valuation, which is the exponent of the prime $p$ in the prime factorization of $q$. Therefore, for example $|12|_2 = 2^{-2} = \frac{1}{4}$. For rational numbers $\frac{a}{b}$, $v_p(\frac{a}{b}) = v_p(a) -v_p(b)$, so for instance, $|\frac{9}{8}|_2 = 2^{-(0-3))} = 2^3 = 8$. 

Now try to think of another norm on $\mathbb{Q}$. It is actually impossible. This is called **Ostrowski's Theorem**:
\begin{theorem}[Ostrowski's Theorem]
Two norms $||\cdot||$ and $||\cdot||_{*}$ are called equivalent if there exists $\lambda \in (0, \infty)$ such that $||x|| = ||x||_{*}^{\lambda}$. Then any (nontrivial) norm $||\cdot||_{*}$ is equivalent to $|\cdot|$ (absolute value) or $|\cdot|_p$ (p-adic norm).
\end{theorem}

I will conclude this article with a proof of the theorem due to Schikhof (2007). The proof only require minimal levels of number theory and analysis. 
\begin{proof}
Let $||\cdot||_{*}$ be a norm defined on the rationals. The proof begins by showing that the values of $||\cdot||_{*}$ is entirely determined by the values it takes on prime numbers. 

From the fact that $1 \times 1 = 1$ and the multiplicity of the norm, $||1||_*^2 = ||1||_*$, making $||1||_*$ equal to 0 or 1. Since $1 \neq 0$, $||1||_* = 1$. A similar argument shows that $||-1||_* = 1$ as well. 

Then for all positive integers $n$, $||-n||_{*} = ||-1||_{*} ||n||_{*} = 1\cdot ||n||_{*} = ||n||_*$. Also, since $n^{-1} \cdot n = 1$, $||n^{-1}||_* \cdot ||n||_* = ||1||_* = 1$, so $||n^{-1}||_* = ||n||_*^{-1}$. 

Now let $r \in \mathbb{Q_{+}}$, then there exists two coprime numbers $p$ and $q$ such that $r = pq^{-1}$, then the properties above show that $||r||_{*} = ||p||_{*} ||q^{-1}||_{*} = ||p||_{*} ||q||_{*}^{-1}$. Altogether, the norm of a positive rational is entirely determined from that of its numerator and denominator.

Finally, let $\mathbb{P}$ be the set of prime numbers. For all positive integer $n$, we can write
\[n = \prod_{p \in \mathbb{P}} p^{v_p(n)}\]
Then by the multiplicity property, 
\[||n||_* = ||\prod_{p \in \mathbb{P}} p^{v_p(n)}||_* = \prod_{p \in \mathbb{P}} ||p||_*^{v_p(n)}\]

Therefore, the norm of any rational number is determined by the norm on the prime factors of the numerator and the denominator. 

Now we continue with two cases:
1. There exists a positive integer $n$ such that $||n||_* > 1$. 
2. For all integers $n$, one has $||n||_* \leq 1$.

### Case 1
 Suppose that there exists a positive integer $n$ such that $||n||_* > 1$. Let $k$ be a non-negative integer and $b$ be a positive integer greater than 
1. We express $n^k$ in base $b$: there exists a positive integer $m$ and integers $(c_i)_{0 \leq i < m}$ such that for all $i$, $0 \leq c_i < b$ and $n^k = \sum_{i<m} c_i b^i$. In particular $n^k \geq b^{m-1}$ so $m \leq 1 + k \log_b n$.

Then for each term $c_i b^i$, $||c_i b^i||_* = ||c_i||_* ||b||_*^i$. Since $c_i$ is a digit, write $c_i = 1+ \dots + 1$, so $||c_i||_* = ||1||_* + \dots + ||1||_* = 1+\dots + 1 = c_i \leq b-1$. Also, $||b||_*^i$ is at most $\max \{1, ||b||_*^{m-1}\}$. Therefore, by the triangle inequality and the above bound on $m$, it follows that $||c_i b^i||_* \leq (b-1) \max \{1, ||b||_*^{m-1}\}$, so 
\begin{align}
||n||_*^k &\leq m \max_{i<m} \{||c_i b^i||_*\} \\ 
&\leq m (b-1) \max \{1, ||b||_*^{m-1}\} \\ 
&\leq (1 + k \log_b n) (b-1) \max \{1, ||b||_*^{k \log_b n}\}
\end{align}
Raising each side to power $k^{-1}$ gives 
\[||n||_* \leq ((1 + k \log_b n) (b-1))^{\frac{1}{k}} \max \{1, ||b||_*^{\log_b n}\}\]
Taking the limit as $k$ goes to $\infty$ on both sides gives 
\[||n||_* \leq \max \{1, ||b||_*^{\log_b n}\}\]

Now since $||n||_* > 1$, the inequality above shows $||b||_* > 1$. As a result, all integers greater than one have a norm strictly greater than one by repeating this argument. Thus generalizing the above, for any choice of integers $n$ and $b$ greater than or equal to 2, we get 
\[||n||_* \leq ||b||_*^{\log_b n}\]
i.e. 
\[\log_n ||n||_* \leq \log_b ||b||_*\]
By symmetry, this inequality is an equality. In particular for all $n \geq 2$, $\log_n ||n||_* = \log_2 ||2||_* = \lambda$, i.e. $||n||_* = n^{\lambda} = |n|^{\lambda}$ where $|\cdot|$ is the normal absolute value. 

As per the above result on the determination of an absolute value by its values on the prime numbers, we easily see that $||r||_* = |r|^{\lambda}$ for all rational $r$, thus demonstrating equivalence to the real absolute value.

### Case 2
Suppose that for all integer $n$, one has $||n||_* \leq 1$. As our absolute value is non-trivial, there must exist a positive integer n for which $||n||_{*}<1$. Decomposing $n$ on the prime numbers shows that there exists $p \in \mathbb{P}$ with $||p||_* < 1$. We claim that in fact this is so for one prime number only.

Suppose by contradiction that $p$ and $q$ are primes with $||p||_* < 1$ and $||q||_* < 1$. Let $k$ be a positive integer such that $||p||_{*}^{k}$ and $||q||_{*}^{k}$ are smaller than $\frac{1}{2}$. Then by Bézout's identity, since $p^k$ and $q^k$ are coprime, there exists integers $a$ and $b$ such that $ap^k + bq^k = 1$. This yields a contradiction since 
\[1 = ||1||_* \leq ||a||_* ||p||_*^k + ||b||_* ||q||_*^k < \frac{||a||_* + ||b||_*}{2} \leq 1\]

This means that there exists a unique prime $p$ such that $||p||_{*}<1$ and that for all other primes $q$, one has $||q||_{*}=1$. Let $\lambda = -\log_p ||p||_*$. Since $||p||_* < 1$, we can infer that $0 < \lambda < \infty$. We finally verify that $|p|_p^\lambda = p^{-\lambda} = ||p||_*$ and for all other primes $q$, $|q|_p^\lambda = 1 = ||q||_*$. As per the above result on the determination of an absolute value by its values on the prime numbers, we conclude that $||r||_* = |r|_p^{\lambda}$ for all rational $r$, implying that this absolute value is equivalent to the p-adic one. 
\end{proof}
In fact, the absolute value is the only Archimedean norm on $\mathbb{Q}$.
summary: An Introduction to Norm Theory and Ostrowski's Theorem
